questions.q: Length, breadth and thickness of a strip having a uniform cross section are measured to be 10.5 cm , 0.05 mm , and $6.0 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, respectively. Which of the following option(s) give(s) the volume of the strip in $\mathrm{cm}^3$ with correct significant figures:
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{L}=10.5 \mathrm{~cm} \rightarrow 3$ significant digits
$\mathrm{b}=0.05 \mathrm{~cm} \rightarrow 1$ significant digit
$\mathrm{t}=6.0 \mu \mathrm{~m} \rightarrow 2$ significant digits
Volume, $\mathrm{V}=$ Lbt must have only 1 significant digit
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{V}=10.5 \times 0.05 \times 10^{-1} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}^3 \\
& =3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{cc}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The dimensions of a cone are measured using a scale with a least count of $2 \mathrm{~mm}$. The diameter of the base and the height are both measured to be $20.0 \mathrm{~cm}$. The maximum percentage error in the determination of the volume is _______ .
questions.solution: $\mathrm{V}=\frac{1}{3} \pi\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)^2 \mathrm{H}$ $\therefore \%$ Error in $\mathrm{V}=2$ (% error in $\mathrm{D})+\%$ error in $\mathrm{H}$. $\because$ Least count is $2 \mathrm{~mm}$. $\therefore \%$ error in D $=\frac{2 \mathrm{~mm}}{20 \mathrm{~cm}} \times 100 \%=1 \%$ & % error in $\mathrm{H}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~mm}}{20 \mathrm{~cm}} \times 100 \%=1 \%$ So $\%$ error in $\mathrm{V}=2 \times 1 \%+1 \%=3 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment for determination of the focal length of a thin convex lens, the distance of the object from the lens is $10 \pm 0 . 1cm$ and the distance of its real image from the lens is $20 \pm 0 . 2cm$. The error in the determination of focal length of the lens is $n %$. The value of $n$ is _____.
questions.solution:
Given:

Object distance $= 10 \pm 0 . 1cm$

Image distance $= 20 \pm 0 . 2cm$

As per lens formula

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{\left(- 10\right)} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$⇒ f = \dfrac{20}{3}cm$

Differentiate equation $\left(i\right)$ on both sides, we get

$\left(- \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}\right)dv - \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{u}^{2}}\right)du = \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{f}^{2}}\right)df$

For calculating maximum error, we will add all values

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{{f}^{2}}df = + \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}dv + \dfrac{1}{{u}^{2}}du$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{df}{f}\right) \times 100 = \left[\left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{{20}^{2}} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{{10}^{2}}\right)\dfrac{20}{3}\right] \times 100$

$= \left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{4} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{1}\right)\dfrac{20}{3} = 1$

Therefore,

$\dfrac{df}{f} \times 100 = 1 % = n$

questions.q: Two capacitors with capacitance values ${C}_{1} = \left(2000 \pm 10\right)pF$  and ${C}_{2} = \left(3000 \pm 15\right)pF$ are connected in series. The voltage applied across this combination is $V = \left(5 . 00 \pm 0 . 02\right)V$. The percentage error in the calculation of the energy stored in this combination of capacitors is __________.
questions.solution:
For the purpose of calculation of error, fundamental formula is considered

$\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{{C}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{C}_{2}} ⇒ C = 1200pF$

$- dC{C}_{1}^{2} = - d{C}_{1}{C}_{1}^{2} - d{C}_{2}{C}_{2}^{2}$

$dC = 6pF$

Equivalent capacitance $= \left(1200 \pm 6\right)pF$

$E = 1 / 2{CV}^{2}$

$( dE / E = dC / C + 2dV / V ) \times 100$

$= 1 . 3 %$

questions.q:
Paragraph: If the measurement errors in all the independent quantities are known, then it is possible to determine the error in any dependent quantity. This is done by the use of series expansion and truncating the expansion at the first power of the error. For example, consider the relation $z = \dfrac{x}{y}$. If the errors in $x, yandzare ∆ x, ∆ yand ∆ z$ , respectively, then

$z \pm ∆ z = \dfrac{x \pm ∆ x}{y \pm ∆ y} = \dfrac{x}{y}\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ x}{x}\right){\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ y}{y}\right)}^{- 1}$

The series expansion for ${\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ y}{y}\right)}^{- 1}$, to first power in $∆ y / y, is1 ∓ \left(∆ y / y\right)$. The relative errors in independent variables are always added. So the error in $z$ will be

$\text{\Delta}z = z( \dfrac{\text{\Delta}x}{x} + \dfrac{\text{\Delta}y}{y} ) .$
The above derivation makes the assumption that \(\Delta r / x \ll 1, \Delta y / y < 1\). Therefore, the higher powers of these quantities are neglected.
Question : Consider the ratio \(r=\frac{(1-a)}{(1+a)}\) to be determined by measuring a dimensionless quantity a If the error in the measurement of a is \(\Delta a(\frac{\Delta a}{a}<<1)\), then what is the error \(\Delta r\) in determining \(r\) ?
questions.solution:
$r = \left(\dfrac{1 - a}{1 + a}\right)$
$\dfrac{∆ r}{r} = \dfrac{∆ \left(1 - a\right)}{\left(1 - a\right)} + \dfrac{∆ \left(1 + a\right)}{\left(1 + a\right)}$
$= \dfrac{∆ a}{\left(1 - a\right)} + \dfrac{∆ a}{\left(1 + a\right)}$
$= \dfrac{∆ a\left(1 + a + 1 - a\right)}{\left(1 - a\right)\left(1 + a\right)}$
$∴ ∆ r = \dfrac{2 ∆ a}{\left(1 - a\right)\left(1 + a\right)}\dfrac{\left(1 - a\right)}{\left(1 + a\right)} = \dfrac{2 ∆ a}{{\left(1 + a\right)}^{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person measures the depth of a well by measuring the time interval between dropping a stone and receiving the sound of impact with the bottom of the well. The error in his measurement of time is $\deltaT = 0.01$ seconds and he measures the depth of the well to be L = 20 meters. Take the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$ and the velocity of sound is $300m{s}^{- 1}$ . Then the fractional error in the measurement, $\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$ , is closest to
questions.solution:
Total time taken,

$T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}} + \dfrac{L}{c}$, $c$ is the sound speed in air.

Now, for an error $\deltaL$ in L,

We have an error $\deltaT$ in T

So, $T + \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(L + \deltaL\right)}{g}} + \dfrac{\left(L + \deltaL\right)}{c}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)} + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

Since, $\dfrac{\deltaT}{T}$ is very small, hence

$\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$ is also small, so taking binomial approximation

$T + \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ T + \deltaT = \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\right) + \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \left(\dfrac{L}{c}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ \deltaT = \left[\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2g}} + \left(\dfrac{L}{c}\right)\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$

$⇒ 0 . 01 = \left[\sqrt{\dfrac{20}{2 \times 10}} + \left(\dfrac{20}{300}\right)\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$

$⇒ 0 . 01 = \left[1 + \dfrac{1}{15}\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L} ⇒ \dfrac{\deltaL}{L} = \dfrac{0 . 15}{16}$

$%error = \left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) \times 100%$

$= \dfrac{15}{16}%$

$\approx 1%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment to determine the acceleration due to gravity g, the formula used for the time period of a periodic motion is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{7\left(R - r\right)}{5g}} .$ The values of R and r are measured to be $\left(60 \pm 1\right)mmand\left(10 \pm 1\right)mm,$ respectively. In five successive measurements, the time period is found to be 0.52s, 0.56s, 0.57s, 0.54s and 0.59s. The least count of the watch used for the measurement of time period is 0.01s. Which of the following statements (s) is (are) true?
options: The error in the measurement of r is 10%.
The error in the measurement of T is 3.57 %.
The error in the measurement of T is 2%.
The error in the determined value of g is 11%.
questions.solution:
T Absolute error
1 0.52 $- 0.04$
2 0.56 00
3 0.57 $+ 0.01$
4 0.54 $- 0.02$
5 0.59 $+ 0.03$
${T}_{avg} = 0.556$ $= 0.56$



Avg. absolute error $\dfrac{0 . 04 + 0 + 0 . 01 + 0 . 02 + 0 . 03}{5} = 0 . 02$
Percentage error in time period$= \dfrac{∆ T}{T} \times 100% = \dfrac{0 . 02}{0 . 56} \times 100% \approx 3.57%$
Percentage error in radius$= \dfrac{∆ r}{r} \times 100% = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 100 = 10%$
Also, $g = \dfrac{28\pi\left(R - r\right)}{5{T}^{2}}$

Percentage error in $g$,=$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} = \dfrac{∆ R + ∆ r}{R - r} + \dfrac{2 ∆ T}{T}$
$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} \times 100% = \dfrac{1 + 1}{50} \times 100% + 2\left(3.57\right)%$$\approx 11%$

questions.q: The energy of a system as a function of time $t$ is given as $E\left(t\right) = {A}^{2}\left(- \alphat\right)$ , where $\alpha = 0.2{s}^{- 1}$ . The measurement of $A$ has an error of 1.25%. If the error in the measurement of time is 1.50%, the percentage error in the value of $E ( t )$ at $t = 5$ s is
questions.solution:
Energy $E = {A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}$
For small % errors, we can, do differentiation
$dE = 2A\left(dA\right){e}^{- \alphat} + {A}^{2}\left(- \alpha{e}^{- \alphat}dt\right)$
Fractional error $= \dfrac{dE}{E} = \dfrac{2A{e}^{- \alphat}\left(dA\right) + \left(- \alpha{A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}\right)dt}{{A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}} = 2\left(\dfrac{dA}{A}\right) + \left(- \alpha\dfrac{dt}{t}\right)t$
% error $= 2\left(1.25%\right) + \left(0.2 \times 1.5%\right) \times 5$
$= 4%$ (errors always add up)
Alternate solution:
$E = {A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}$
Taking natural logarithm on both sides,
$ln\left(E\right) = ln\left({A}^{2}\right) + \left(- \alphat\right)$
Differentiating
$\dfrac{dE}{E} = 2\left(\dfrac{dA}{A}\right) + \left(- \alphadt\right)$
For small fractional erros, errors always add up
$\left|\dfrac{dE}{E}\right| = 2\left|\dfrac{dA}{A}\right| + \alpha\left(\dfrac{dt}{t}\right) \times t$
$= 2\left(1.25%\right) + \left(0.2\right)\left(1.5%\right)5$
$= 4%$

The wavelength $\lambda$~is exactly known and the error in& $\theta$ is constant for all the values of~$\theta$. As $\text{\theta}$~increases from $0 °$,
options: the absolute error in $d$ remains constant.
the fractional error in $d$ remains constant.

$2d\text\sin\theta = \lambda$
$d = \dfrac{\lambda}{\text{2 sin}\theta}$
Differentiate on both the sides,
$∂ \left(d\right) = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} ∂ \left(\text{cosec}\theta\right)$
$∂ \left(d\right) = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\left(- \text{cosec}\theta\text{cot}\theta\right) ∂ \theta$
$∂ \left(d\right) = \dfrac{- \lambda\text\cos\theta}{2{\text\sin}^{2}\theta} ∂ \theta$
$\theta =$increases and $\dfrac{\lambda\text\cos\theta}{2{\text\sin}^{2}\theta}$ decreases.
Alternate solution
$d = \dfrac{\lambda}{\text{2 sin}\theta}$
$ℓnd = ℓn\lambda - ℓn2 - ℓn\text\sin\theta$
$\dfrac{\Delta \left(d\right)}{d} = 0 - 0 - \dfrac{1}{\text\sin\theta} \times \text\cos\theta\left(\Delta \text{\theta}\right)$
Fractional error, $\left|+ \left(d\right)\right| = \left|\text{cot}\theta \Delta \theta\right|$
Absolute error, $\Delta d = \left(d\text{cot}\theta\right) \Delta \theta$
$\dfrac{d}{2\text\sin\theta} \times \dfrac{\text\cos\theta}{\text\sin\theta}$
$\Delta d = \dfrac{\text\cos\theta}{{\text\sin}^{2}\theta}$

questions.q: In the determination of Young's modulus $\left(Y=\frac{4 M L g}{\pi l d^{2}}\right)$ by using Searle's method, a wire of length $L=2 \mathrm{~m}$ and diameter $d=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ is used. For a load $M=2.5 \mathrm{~kg}$, an extension $l=0.25 \mathrm{~mm}$ in the length of the wire is observed. Quantities $d and l$ are measured using a screw gauge and a micrometer, respectively. They have the same pitch of $0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$. The number of divisions on their circular scale is 100 . The contributions to the maximum probable error of the $Y$ measurement
options: due to the errors in the measurements of $d$ and $l$ are the same.
due to the error in the measurement of $d$ is twice that due to the error in the measurement of $l$.
due to the error in the measurement of $l$ is twice that due to the error in the measurement of $d$.
due to the error in the measurement of $d$ is four times that due to the error in the measurement of $l$.
questions.solution:
The maximum possible error in $Y$ due to $l$ and $d \frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=\frac{\Delta l}{l}+\frac{2 \Delta d}{d}$ Least count $=\frac{\text{ Pitch }}{\text{ No. of division on circular scale }} =\frac{0.5}{100} \mathrm{~mm}=0.005 \mathrm{~mm}$

Here, $\Delta d=\Delta l=0.005 \mathrm{~mm}$

Error contribution of $l=\frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{0.005 \mathrm{~mm}}{0.25 \mathrm{~mm}}=\frac{1}{50}$

Error contribution of

$d=\frac{2 \Delta d}{d}=\frac{2 \times 0.005 \mathrm{~mm}}{0.5 \mathrm{~mm}}=\frac{1}{50}$

Hence contribution to the maximum possible error in the measurement of $y$ due to $l$ and $d$ is the same.

questions.q: The density of a solid ball is to be determined in an experiment. The diameter of the ball is measured with a screw gauge, whose pitch is $0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ and there are 50 divisions on the circular scale. The reading on the main scale is $2.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ and that on the circular scale is 20 divisions. If the measured mass of the ball has a relative error of $2 \%$, the relative percentage error in the density is
questions.solution:
Least count of screw gauge $=\frac{0.5}{50}$
=0.01 $\mathrm{~mm}=\Delta$r

Diameter, $r=2.5 \mathrm{~mm}+20 \times \frac{0.5}{50}$
=270 $\mathrm{~mm}

\frac{\Delta r}{r}=\frac{0.01}{2.70}$or $\frac{\Delta r}{r} \times 100=\frac{1}{2.7}$
Now, density $d=\frac{m}{V}=\frac{m}{\frac{4}{3} \pi\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^3}$
Here, $r$ is the diameter.

$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad$$\frac{\Delta d}{d}$& $\times$100=$\left$\{$\frac{\Delta m}{m}+$3$\left(\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right)\right$\} $\times$100 \\
= & $\frac{\Delta m}{m} \times$100+3 $\times\left(\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right) \times$100
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned}$& =2 \%+3 $\times \frac{1}{27}$\\
& =3.11 \%
\end{aligned}

Analysis of Question
(i) Question is moderately difficult.
(ii) In practical part, questions in JEE are asked from vernier callipers and screw gauge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student uses a simple pendulum of exactly $1 \mathrm{~m}$ length to determine $g$, the acceleration due to gravity. He uses a stop watch with the least count of $1 \mathrm{~s}$ for this and records $40 \mathrm{~s}$ for 20 oscillations. For this observation, which of the following statement(s) is/are true?
options:
Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period, is $0.05 \mathrm{~s}$

Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period, is $1 \mathrm{~s}$

Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is $5 \%$

Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is $2.5 \%$
questions.solution:
$T=\frac{40 \mathrm{~s}}{20}=2 \mathrm{~s}$.
Further, t=n T=20 T or $\Delta t=20 \Delta T\therefore \quad \frac{\Delta t}{t}=\frac{\Delta T}{T}
or \Delta T=\frac{T}{t} \cdot \Delta t=\left(\frac{2}{40}\right)(1)=0.05 \mathrm{~s}$
Further, $T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ or $\quad T \propto g^{-1 / 2}$
\therefore $\frac{\Delta T}{T} \times$100=-$\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\Delta g}{g} \times$100

or $\%$ error in determination of $g$ is

$\begin{aligned}\frac{\Delta g}{g} \times$100 & =-200 $\times \frac{\Delta T}{T}$\\
& =-$\frac{200 \times 0.05}{2}=-$5 \%
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ correct options are (a) and (c).

questions.q: A student performs an experiment to determine the Young's modulus of a wire, exactly $2 \mathrm{~m}$ long, by Searle's method. In a particular reading, the student measures the extension in the length of the wire to be $0.8 \mathrm{~mm}$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.05 \mathrm{~mm}$ at a load of exactly $1.0 \mathrm{~kg}$. The student also measures the diameter of the wire to be $0.4 \mathrm{~mm}$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.01 \mathrm{~mm}$. Take $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ (exact). The Young's modulus obtained from the reading is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} Y & =\frac{F L}{A l}=\frac{4 F L}{\pi d^2 l} \\ & =\frac{(4)(1.0 \times 9.8)(2)}{\pi\left(0.4 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2\left(0.8 \times 10^{-3}\right)}=20 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2\end{aligned}$
Further $\quad \frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=2  \left(\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right)+\left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\right)
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \Delta Y & = \left\{2\left(\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right)+\left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\right)\right \}Y= \left\{2 \times \frac{0.01}{0.4}+\frac{0.05}{0.8}\right\} \times2.0 \times10^{11} \\
& =0.2 \times10^{11}  \mathrm{ N}/  \mathrm{m}^2 \text{$ or $}}(Y+\Delta Y)=(2+0.2) \times10^{11}  \mathrm{ N}/  \mathrm{m}^2
\end{aligned}$ The correct option is (b).

questions.q: A student performs an experiment for determination of $g\left(=\frac{4 \pi^2 l}{T^2}\right), l \approx 1 \mathrm{~m}$, and he commits an error of $\Delta l$. For $T$ he takes the time of $n$ oscillations with the stop watch of least count $\Delta T$ and he commits a human error of $0.1 \mathrm{~s}$. For which of the following data, the measurement of $g$ will be most accurate?
options:
$\Delta L=0.5, \Delta T=0.1, n=20$

$\Delta L=0.5, \Delta T=0.1, n=50$

$\Delta L=0.5, \Delta T=0.01, n=20$

$\Delta L=0.1, \Delta T=0.05, n=50$
questions.solution:
$\frac{\Delta g}{g}=\frac{\Delta l}{l}+2 \frac{\Delta T}{n}$
In option (d) error in $\Delta g$ is minimum and number of observations made are maximum. Hence, in this case error in $g$ will be minimum.
